episodes.183446: Severe storms fired up along a backdoor front moving south and west across eastern NM. One of these storms produced golf ball sized hail near Ramon along U.S. Highway 285.
episodes.183577: A deamplifying mid level shortwave with dewpoints in the 70s and decent instability brought scattered thunderstorms and widespread flash flooding to Massachusetts and Rhode Island. There were many streets closed, many cars stranded in flood waters, and several houses with flooded basements or first floors.
episodes.183578: A deamplifying mid level shortwave with dewpoints in the 70s and decent instability brought scattered thunderstorms and widespread flash flooding to Rhode Island and Massachusetts. There were many streets closed, many cars stranded in flood waters, and several houses with flooded basements or first floors.
episodes.183620: A slow moving thunderstorm caused flooding in Greene County during the evening of the 10th.
episodes.183759: A couple rounds of severe thunderstorms occurred on the evening of the tenth. A stalled out outflow boundary was located from roughly Vigo Park (Swisher County) to Jayton (Kent County). Enhanced upslope flow along the edge of the caprock and strong instabilities generated an isolated severe supercell in Swisher County producing hail up to quarter size. The second round of severe thunderstorms initiated in eastern New Mexico and moved into the South Plains late in the evening hours. A southerly low level jet enhanced moisture advection and elevated instability allowing these storms to persist across the region. Severe thunderstorm winds were reported in Parmer County and Garza County along with wind damage in Hall County.
episodes.183761: An approaching cold front interacted with strong instability creating a broken line of thunderstorms across the central South Plains into the central Rolling Plains. One of these storms became severe as it moved across King County producing a wind gust to 64 mph.
episodes.184025: Thunderstorms produced locally heavy rain in southwestern New Jersey on the evening of September 10.  Rainfall totals were as high as 3 to 5 inches.
episodes.184145: Thunderstorms produced locally heavy rain in central New Jersey on the afternoon and evening of September 11.  Rainfall totals were as high as 1 to 2 inches.
episodes.184351: As hurricane Lee moved well north of the region, external feeding bands from the hurricane reached the local islands. Additionally, the moisture advected into the region, contributed to the development of strong showers along the Cordillera Central and southern Puerto Rico. A few flooding reports, and even a funnel cloud was detected within this activity.
episodes.184592: A stalled front remains situated just to the northwest this morning with a light onshore flow near the surface while persistent southwesterly flow continues aloft. Cooler than normal mid-level temperatures created deeper instability that strengthened diurnally driven sea breeze storms as they develop along the east-coast sea breeze in the afternoon. Deeper moisture was across NE FL and portions of SE GA (generally south and east of Waycross) created more widespread storm coverage, especially along and west of the St Johns River basin as the sea breeze interacted with the river breeze. ||Strong to marginally severe wind gusts of 40-60 mph occurred. Marginal deep layer shear was around 20 kts which create a lower end hail threat. Locally heavy rainfall occurred that created mainly nuisance minor flood issues.

episodes.184744: Training showers and thunderstorms developed along a slow moving frontal boundary stretching from Connecticut to Southwest Maine on the evening of the 11th. The anomalously moist airmass caused moderate to heavy widespread rain of 1 to 3 inches. A localized axis of heavy rainfall between 4 to 6 inches extended from central Massachusetts across the Stateline and into Nashua, New Hampshire. Flash flooding developed over Nashua, Hollis, and Hudson with numerous water rescues and flooded basements.
episodes.184885: A complex of thunderstorms developed across the eastern New Mexico Plains and moved into northern portions of the Permian Basin resulting in isolated strong to severe wind gusts.
episodes.185072: Severe thunderstorms produced wind damage and quarter size hail around the Orlando metro area.
episodes.185133: Heavy rain primarily impacted the I-25 corridor in southern Colorado. No reports of flash flooding.
episodes.185256: Heavy thunderstorms developed in an unstable and moist environment on September 11th, 2023 and produced flash flooding in New York. Thunderstorms developed along a stationary front that was draped over the area in an environment with 2000-2500 J/kg of SBCAPE and 1.7-1.9 inches of PWAT. The thunderstorms produced rainfall rates of 1 to 2 inches per hour and a total of 1-3 inches of rainfall in a couple of hours.
episodes.185257: Heavy thunderstorms developed in an unstable and moist environment on September 11th, 2023 and produced flash flooding in Connecticut. The thunderstorms produced rainfall rates of 1 to 2 inches per hour and a total of 1-3 inches of rainfall in a couple of hours.
episodes.185564: The combination of an upper level trough of low pressure moving across the area and some instability resulted in a few severe thunderstorms. The severe storms produced large hail and damaging winds.
episodes.185572: A warm front moved eastward towards the Kentucky border counties during the day on September 9th, 2023. It then stalled during the afternoon and evening along the highest terrain just east of the state. Showers and thunderstorms developed just ahead of this front and moved westward into eastern Kentucky. As the front stalled, the storms began back-building and training across some of the same areas. Bell County was the hardest hit in eastern Kentucky, receiving over 3.5 inches in a 2 hour time period. Multiple instances of flash flooding were reported as a result.
episodes.185586: A good bit of moisture worked its way into the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles on the 9th through the 11th. The upper level pattern favored upper level help for storms to travel into the combined Panhandles from the west and northwest during the late afternoon into overnight hours. The first night on the 9th a couple of strong supercell thunderstorms dropped hail up to 2.5 in diameter in the western Oklahoma Panhandle. More widespread storms managed to drop hail up to 1.5, but these storms also produced several severe wind gusts upwards of 80 plus mph on the night of the 10th across much of the combined Panhandles.

episodes.185796: Scattered thunderstorms in advance of a frontal boundary produced heavy rain which caused flash flooding across portions of eastern Virginia.
episodes.185821: A boundary near the coast resulted in a few showers and thunderstorms popping up. One storm produced a tornado in southern Delaware.
episodes.185878: Thunderstorms once again formed along a stationary frontal boundary positioned over northeastern Pennsylvania and brought localized flash flooding to the region.
episodes.185879: Thunderstorms formed along a stationary frontal boundary extending from northeastern Pennsylvania into eastern New York which brought localized flash flooding to the region.
episodes.185894: A flash flood event occurred in the Duluth area during the late evening of September 11th into the early morning hours of the 12th. An area of thunderstorms developed over Duluth during the evening hours and continued to backbuild over the hillside for a few hours before another area of rainfall pushed in from the west and helped push the backbuilding storms out over the lake. Rainfall totals of 3 to 6 inches fell over a small area at the top of the Duluth hillside in the Chester Creek basin in the area around College of St. Scholastica. This sent a surge of water downstream on Chester Creek down the Duluth hillside just to the east of downtown. The creek is generally underground for most of its run down the hill to Lake Superior, but the volume of water overwhelmed the tunnels and led to fast-flowing water on the surface. This resulted in a a few rescues by the fire department as the water cut-off access to an apartment building. At the bottom of the hill, Interstate 35 runs through a series of tunnels and the runoff from Chester Creek collected in the tunnels leading to a closure of the highway for a few hours until the water subsided.
episodes.185989: Isolated thunderstorm developed along a stationary boundary across Middle GA. A couple storms were able to tap into some weaker instability and become strong. Only a couple of damaging wind reports were recorded.
episodes.186113: A convective cloud line developed near and just south of the Lower Florida Keys.  A couple waterspouts were observed.
episodes.186146: Isolated showers and thunderstorms developed each afternoon during the weekend of 9-10 September, mainly over areas south of US-50. Subtropical moisture steadily flowing north along the western periphery of a longwave ridge centered over the US/Mexico border moistened mid-levels across southern portions of our CWA increased storm chances to 20-30%. Hazards included stronger outflow winds, frequent lightning, localized areas of heavy rainfall, and the increased chance for small hail in stronger storm cores.
episodes.186176: Isolated to scattered thunderstorms developed along the sea breeze in the afternoon hours and moved toward the coast, producing strong wind gusts in Charleston Harbor.
episodes.186177: Isolated to scattered thunderstorms developed in the afternoon and early evening hours along the sea breeze and ahead of an inland station front across portions of southeast South Carolina. A few of these thunderstorms became strong enough to produce damaging wind gusts and small hail.
episodes.186191: A cold front and mid-level shortwave slowly moved through the area. Thunderstorms formed along the front and one became severe as it moved over the waters.

An EF-0 tornado occurred on the afternoon of September 11, 2023, in the Dagsboro area of Sussex County, Delaware. |The brief tornado began along Adams Road just east of Dagsboro where damage to multiple structures and trees was observed. A shed in a backyard of a home on Adams Road had partial roof and wall collapse, and an additional larger and more structurally sound shed just feet from the first one was shifted off of its foundation, had the door blown off, and had partial roof collapse. Damage to three homes along Adams Road was noted with glass windows blown out and partial siding and shingle loss. Numerous |large softwood trees were uprooted along the wood line behind the homes on Adams Road along and had large branches snapped off of the trunks.||Further south on Adams Road, very close to the intersection of Tingle Lane, minor loss of siding was noted on a home as well as some more tree and limb damage. This is likely where the tornado reached its maximum width of around 370 yards.||The tornado then continued a short distance down Piney Neck Road to near the intersection of Wild Goose Way where another softwood tree was uprooted in the backyard of a home. The tornado likely occluded at this point and lifted as no further damage was found further downstream.||The National Weather Service would like to thank Sussex County Emergency Management Agency, local Skywarn spotter coordinators, and the public for their assistance with this survey.
